_readme: Real-sounding posts the linter must NEVER flag — this half protects users from false positives, which are worse than misses (a founder whose genuine voice gets flagged stops trusting the product). These 30 are hand-written seeds; REPLACE/AUGMENT them with the user's real approved posts over time — that's the actual wedge protection. Entries with a 'note' are deliberate near-misses that sit just outside a pattern's boundary; if a pattern edit starts catching them, the eval tells you before a user does.

samples.text: Spent the morning re-reading support tickets from our first ten customers. Half our roadmap was sitting right there the whole time.
We killed a feature 40 people loved to save the one thousand who were confused by it. Still thinking about those 40 emails.
My cofounder asked me why our churn dropped in March. I checked the data. We didn't ship anything in March. We just answered support faster.

samples.note: near-miss: 'it's not X, but it's Y' — the 'but' breaks the parallel-contrast pattern; genuine humility phrasing must survive
samples.text: It's not much, but it's a start — 12 paying customers, all from word of mouth.

samples.note: near-miss: 'honestly' is fine; only the announced 'I'll be honest' construction is the tell
samples.text: Honestly, the best marketing we ever did was rewriting our onboarding emails at 1am after a customer call that stung.
Hiring lesson from this year: slow down on the resume, speed up on the reference calls. References told me everything twice.
I used to write 2,000-word essays nobody read. Now I write 200-word notes people forward to their teams. Shorter forced me to actually have a point.
The demo crashed twice in front of our biggest prospect. They signed anyway. People buy the way you recover, apparently.
Three years in and I still get nervous publishing. The day that stops is probably the day I've started writing for the algorithm instead of the reader.
Our best channel is embarrassingly boring. We answer questions on forums where our customers already hang out. That's it. That's the strategy.

samples.note: near-miss: 'fast-paced' alone is legitimate; only the full 'in today's fast-paced world' opener is the tell
samples.text: Agency life is fast-paced by design, and I stopped apologizing for loving the speed.

samples.note: near-miss: 'ever-evolving' without the 'in the' framing is legitimate
samples.text: Our pricing page stays ever-evolving; we've rewritten it six times this year and each rewrite taught us who we're actually for.
A customer described our product back to me better than our homepage does. I asked if I could steal her words. She said yes. Conversion went up.
I blocked my calendar for deep work and then spent the block reorganizing my task manager. The system was never the problem.
We raised nothing. We hit profitability at month 14 on a spreadsheet and stubbornness. Default alive changes every conversation you have.
The intern asked why we do standups. Nobody had a good answer. We cancelled them for a month as an experiment. Shipping went up.

samples.note: near-miss: the dramatic-reveal tell requires the colon; the em-dash form is currently allowed — if that changes, this sample forces the decision to be deliberate
samples.text: That's when it hit me — we'd been optimizing a funnel nobody was entering.
Wrote 100 cold emails by hand before automating anything. The replies taught me our pitch. The automation just scaled what already worked.
You can tell a lot about a company by its empty states. Ours used to say 'No data'. Now they teach you the next step. Small screens, big signal.
Every pivot we made started as a support ticket we almost ignored.
I turned down a partnership that would have doubled our traffic. Their audience wasn't our buyer. Growth that doesn't convert is just a hosting bill.
My writing rule after six years of editing other people's posts is simple. Cut the first paragraph. It was warmup. The post starts at paragraph two.
We lost the deal to a worse product with better onboarding. Sat with that one for a while. Then we rebuilt ours in two weeks.
Nobody on my team knew our top three customers by name. Fixed that this week. Everyone ships differently when the user has a face.

samples.note: near-miss: 'the truth about' is legitimate; only the 'here's the truth:' reveal is the tell
samples.text: The truth about our overnight launch success is that it took eleven months of unglamorous groundwork nobody tweeted about.
Asked ten users what they'd pay before writing a line of code. Eight laughed. Two pulled out a card. Built it for the two.
I keep a folder of rejection emails. Re-read it the week we crossed $10k MRR. Growth is quiet revenge done politely.
Stop hiring for culture fit, start hiring for culture add. I know how that sounds. But the quietest hire we made rewrote how we run retros.
Shipped a pricing change at 9am, rolled it back by noon, shipped the fixed version Friday. Customers noticed the speed more than the mistake.
Six drafts of this post and the final version is basically the voice memo I sent my cofounder on Tuesday. Should have started there.

samples.note: near-miss: negation and an 'it's' clause in the SAME post but different sentences — the widened contrast patterns must stay within one sentence
samples.text: The pricing page isn't finished. It's been six months and I still can't explain the middle tier without drawing a diagram.

samples.note: near-miss: 'isn't X, but it's Y' — the 'but' breaks the parallel contrast the same way pass-004 does; genuine concession must survive the widened pattern
samples.text: The dashboard isn't pretty, but it's the first thing three customers asked us not to change.

samples.note: near-miss: a legitimate semicolon between two clauses where the second does NOT reframe the first
samples.text: We rewrote the onboarding in a week; the support tickets about step three stopped within two days of shipping it.

samples.note: near-miss: 'driven' and 'world' both present but not in the buzzword landscape-speak construction
samples.text: She's the most driven engineer I've worked with, and the only one who consistently tells me when a deadline is fantasy.

samples.note: near-miss: 'power' and 'potential' used concretely, outside the harness/unlock stock phrases
samples.text: I underestimated the potential of our smallest customers. Two of them referred more business last year than our biggest logo ever did.
